title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
content:
The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches.

Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred.

title: Donate Equity to Support Digital Rights: Stocks, DAFs, and Giving
content:
Do the holidays have you thinking about how you can support your favorite nonprofit?  

For 35 years, the Electronic Frontier Foundation has been advancing our digital rights, including defending security researchers, encrypting the web, and fighting illegal surveillance. Donating equity to EFF can help support this important work. 

Perhaps your family has taken advantage of the new tax law around giving by creating a Donor-Advised Fund.  

Perhaps your employer has gone public and you now own stock.  

Perhaps you’ve seen some of EFF’s recent successes and thought, Man, imagine what they could do with more. 

A gift of equity can help your contribution go farther and offer tax savings. When you donate appreciated stock, you avoid paying capital gains tax on any increase in its value. You also receive a charitable income tax deduction for the fair market value of appreciated stock on the date it is transferred. Also, more and more companies are offering gift-matching programs that can double your impact at no additional cost.
snippet: Do the holidays have you thinking about how you can support your favorite nonprofit?
creator: Hudson Hongo

title: Amazon Ring’s New Indoor Surveillance Drone Is Not Compatible with Privacy
content:
Amazon Ring has finally announced their long-dreaded indoor drone, a small flying surveillance device connected to their security suite of products that can fly around your house filming and recording things. The device is supposedly designed to fly preset paths across your home and will also activate if a sensor or alarm has been triggered.  

Customers should think twice about purchasing these devices for a number of reasons. These devices are problematic in many of the ways we’ve said Ring’s stationary home surveillance products are a problem, plus some new ways. At a very basic level, they are essentially a window into your house that can be accessed by anyone with access to your account—which has historically included bad actors looking to embarrass or harass Ring users and employees of the company.

title: Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again)
content:
Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did.

Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants, rings, and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long.

Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps, collaborative software, or your cloud backup solutions, have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are all now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game.
snippet: Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did.
creator: Thorin Klosowski

title: 🤕 Medicare's AI Experiment | EFFector 38.20
content:
When we need medical care, we expect decisions about our treatment to be made by our doctors, not a tech company's algorithm. But in January, the federal government launched a program that uses AI to evaluate Medicare beneficiaries' requests for certain procedures.

EFF sued for records on WISeR, seeking badly needed transparency about Medicare's AI experiment. In our latest EFFector newsletter, we're talking about what happens when the government outsources treatment approval to private AI companies—without sufficient transparency, testing, or legal limits.

JOIN OUR NEWSLETTER

For over 35 years, EFFector has been your guide to understanding the intersection of technology, civil liberties, and the law. This issue covers unconstitutional digital dragnets, a post office surveillance scheme, and what EFF uncovered about Medicare's AI experiment.

Prefer to listen in? EFFector is now available on all major podcast platforms. This time we're talking to EFF's Lena Cohen about WISeR records documenting improper denials, operational chaos, and lengthy delays that have left patients waiting in pain. title: We’re Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches
content:
Today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.

Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places.

title: Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents
content:
The number of petitions being filed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has collapsed. That’s not reason for celebration. The PTAB is an important line of defense against low-quality software patents being used in lawsuits against people and companies.

The drop didn’t happen because suddenly patents have become higher quality. It’s simply because USPTO leadership is increasingly refusing to consider good challenges to patents, for reasons unrelated to the merits. The process has become so unreliable that many would-be patent challengers aren’t even trying.

Inter partes review (IPR) is a process that allows people to challenge patents at the Patent Office, rather than having to fight an expensive lawsuit in federal court. It’s one of the most important ways to get bad patents out of the system.

In the third quarter of 2026, July through September, only 97 IPR petitions were filed at the PTAB, compared to 327 petitions during the same period in 2025. Similarly, only 37 IPR petitions were filed in September 2026, compared to 129 petitions in December 2024—the last full month before the current USPTO leadership began reshaping how the Board handles patent challenges.

title: U.S. Supreme Court Deals Final Blow to Corporate Human Rights Accountability
content:
For the past two decades, the U.S. Supreme Court has been slowly weakening the Alien Tort Statute (ATS), a key human rights law that allows foreign nationals to sue persons or entities in civil court for harms resulting from violations of international law. The court’s recent ruling in Cisco Systems, Inc. v. Doe I dealt the law a final blow, foreclosing—absent new legislation by Congress—any future ability by plaintiffs to use the law to hold technology companies accountable for aiding and abetting human rights abuses. EFF filed multiple amicus briefs in the case, including most recently in the Supreme Court.

The ATS was passed by the very first Congress in 1789 and in just a few words gives U.S. federal courts jurisdiction to hear civil claims brought by foreign nationals against defendants who violated “the law of nations or a treaty of the United States." There has been a longstanding question about what counts as a valid civil claim under “the law of nations.”
snippet: For the past two decades, the U.S. Supreme Court has been slowly weakening the Alien Tort Statute (ATS), a key human rights law that allows foreign nationals to sue persons or entities in civil court

title: Google Forcing AI on Students Is BS
content:
Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school.

Students, teachers, and parents across the U.S. are now years into an argument about how schools should respond to the growth of AI-enabled tools. Google decided to skip this debate and take this choice from schools. In August it activated AI chatbot Gemini for 150 million K-12 students on Google Classroom, leaving educators scrambling to respond. A few months later, Google introduced a new way to turn it off — but now administrators would also be turning off Google search.

Google walked this back somewhat, clarifying that Gemini, Gemini notebook, and Search will have their own controls and will be off by default. But because of Google’s broader approach to force AI on all search users, this change is still an example of a tech monopolist pushing unwanted changes into the classroom.

title: Presenting 'Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures'
content:
What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real?

Building a freer, more inclusive digital age requires not only challenging systems of surveillance and control, but also making space for creativity, community, and radical imagination. 

That's why earlier this year with the queer arts collective, we put out a call for submissions inviting people to explore the intersections of technology, identity, and digital liberation—whether that involved pointing the lens towards an underrepresented issue in digital justice efforts; sharing personal accounts of joy, pleasure, or sorrow under surveillance; or painting wide imaginations for our communities using technology for good instead of carcerality and doom.

And we’re excited to share that the project is now live! Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures explores a digital world that dreams wilder and exists louder. Seven artists share their visions of digital liberation, spanning from early internet-coded yearning to escapist steamy chat rooms and seed-laced battle suits for revolution.
snippet: What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real?
creator: Paige Collings
